Causality. The relationship between cause and effect—the principle that one thing brings about or necessitates another through some mechanism, force, or connection. Causality is essential to science and common sense, yet philosophers have vigorously debated what causation truly is and whether it is a real feature of nature.

David Hume famously challenged the view that we directly perceive causal necessity. He argued that we only observe the constant conjunction of events, followed by mental habit. We see that fire is always followed by heat, so we learn to expect heat when we see fire. But Hume questioned whether we actually perceive the necessary causation itself, or merely a pattern. Kant responded to Hume by arguing that causality is not something we perceive directly in the world, but rather a structure imposed by the human mind. Causality, on Kant's view, is an a priori structure of human understanding—a category that organizes experience rather than existing in things themselves.

Causality underlies the logic of scientific explanation. Science seeks causal laws governing natural phenomena. Determinism claims that causality is universal—every event has prior causes and the future is determined by the past. But quantum mechanics has challenged classical causality by introducing fundamental indeterminacy. At the subatomic level, causation appears probabilistic, not deterministic.

The relationship between causality and free will is central to philosophy of action. If all events are causally determined, can human choices be genuinely free? That remains one of philosophy's deepest puzzles. Additionally, philosophers distinguish between different types of causation. Efficient causality is one thing producing an effect—the most obvious kind. But there is also formal causality, material causality, and final causality, expanding our understanding beyond simple mechanical cause-and-effect models.
